q: Which nail is used to install asphalt shingles?
n: Asphalt shingles are commonly fastened with roofing staples (wire staples) driven by a pneumatic stapler into the plywood deck, or with short large-head roofing nails. Source: Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association (ARMA) installation guide.

q: What is considered the most important innovation in asphalt shingles?
n: Algae and moss staining is the chief durability problem of shingles in humid climates. Copper or zinc granules that resist moss and algae growth are a major shingle innovation. Source: ARMA, Algae discoloration of roofs; shingle manufacturer literature.

q: Which component makes asphalt shingles waterproof?
n: Asphalt saturates the fiberglass or felt mat and coats both sides, and it is this asphalt that makes the shingle waterproof. The granules protect it from UV. Source: ASTM D3462 (asphalt shingles); ARMA.

q: Which roofing uses marine plywood as an underlayment and needs heat to seal?
n: Asphalt shingles are nailed over a continuous marine plywood deck with underlayment. Their self-sealing asphalt strips soften in the sun's heat and bond the tabs down. Source: ARMA Residential Asphalt Roofing Manual.

q: What roof slope suits asphalt shingles?
n: Asphalt shingles are a water-shedding (lapped) roofing and need a steep slope, at least 4:12 normally (2:12 with double underlayment). Low and flat roofs need membranes. Source: ARMA Residential Asphalt Roofing Manual; IBC Sec. 1507.2.

q: What fastens GI roofing sheets to steel purlins?
n: Self-drilling, self-tapping (Tek) screws with EPDM washers drill and tap into steel purlins and seal the hole. Source: Metal roofing manufacturer installation guides.

q: Where is GI flashing NOT typically needed?
n: Where two roofing sheets overlap end to end, the lap and sealant seal the joint and no flashing is needed. Flashing is for junctions such as walls, gutters, ridges and valleys. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual.

q: What is the usual remedy for an overflowing valley gutter?
n: An overflowing valley gutter is undersized for the runoff it collects, so the remedy is to enlarge the gutter (and, if needed, its outlets) to the design rainfall. Source: National Plumbing Code of the Philippines (roof drainage sizing); SMACNA gutter sizing.

q: What is the most common roofing in the Philippines?
n: Galvanized iron (corrugated GI and long-span pre-painted steel) is the most common roofing in the Philippines: cheap, light and easy to install. Source: PSA Census of Population and Housing (roof materials of housing units).

q: What is a common mistake in roofing installation?
n: Most roof leaks happen at junctions: walls, valleys, chimneys and penetrations. Poorly lapped or sealed flashing there is the most common installation mistake. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual; NRCA Roofing Manual.

q: What is the ideal roofing for a warehouse?
n: Warehouses have large, simple roofs, and long-span GI sheets cover big spans quickly and cheaply with few laps. Source: Metal roofing manufacturer literature; Time-Saver Standards (warehouses).

q: What is suitable roofing for a sidewalk canopy?
n: Curvilinear (curved) roof sheets are roll-curved metal sheets suited to light arched canopies over sidewalks and walkways. Source: Philippine metal roofing manufacturer product literature.

q: What type of roofing material is best suited for a rest house located near the beach?
n: Asphalt shingles do not rust, so for a beach rest house they avoid the salt-air corrosion that attacks GI sheets. Source: ARMA; metal roofing manufacturer corrosion guidance for coastal sites.

q: What is the most suitable roofing material for a house located in a coastal area?
n: Fired clay tiles are unaffected by salt spray and do not corrode, so they are well suited to coastal houses where metal roofing rusts quickly. Source: Roof tile manufacturer literature; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What roof type best suits the Philippine climate?
n: A hip roof slopes on all four sides. It resists typhoon uplift better than gables (no tall gable wall) and its eaves shade every wall. Source: DPWH/Philippine housing guidelines on typhoon-resistant design; Olgyay, Design with Climate.

q: What is the most effective roof insulation arrangement?
o: Roof sheet, an air gap, then foil insulation
Roof sheet with foil directly underneath
Roof sheet, foil, then an air gap
n: Reflective foil works by low emissivity, so it must face an air space. The best arrangement is roof sheet, then an air gap, then foil, which blocks radiant heat before it reaches the ceiling. Source: ASHRAE Handbook, Fundamentals (reflective insulation); manufacturer literature.

q: Where is roof insulation best placed?
o: Above the purlins, below the roof sheet
n: Roof insulation is best laid over the purlins, directly under the roof sheet, so heat is stopped at the roof before it reaches the attic and ceiling. Source: Philippine Green Building Code (2015), roof insulation; insulation manufacturer guides.

q: What is the main purpose of the air gap in a roof insulation system?
n: The air gap lets the low-emissivity foil block radiant heat, reducing heat transfer into the building. Without the gap the foil only conducts. Source: ASHRAE Handbook, Fundamentals (reflective insulation and air spaces).

q: Which insulation reflects radiant heat from roofing?
n: Aluminum foil insulation has very low emittance and reflects about 95% of radiant heat from a hot roof. Foams and fibers resist conduction instead. Source: ASHRAE Handbook, Fundamentals; ASTM C1313 (radiant barriers).

q: Which roof color absorbs the least heat in the tropics?
n: White roofs have the highest solar reflectance and emit heat well, so they absorb the least solar heat. Source: Philippine Green Building Code (2015); US DOE Cool Roofs guidance.

q: What is the ideal roofing for a greenhouse?
n: Polycarbonate sheets transmit and diffuse daylight, resist hail and impact, and can be UV-coated, so they are the standard greenhouse roofing. Source: Polycarbonate sheet manufacturer literature.

q: What do polycarbonate suppliers often fail to mention?
o: Water wicks into the cells, letting moss grow
n: Multi-wall polycarbonate has hollow flutes that take in water and dust if the ends are not sealed with tape and end caps, causing algae and moss inside. Suppliers often omit this. Source: Polycarbonate sheet manufacturer installation guides.

q: What is a major advantage of polycarbonate roofing for greenhouses?
o: It diffuses natural light while filtering UV
n: UV-protected polycarbonate admits diffused natural light for plant growth while filtering harmful UV, which also protects the sheet. Source: Polycarbonate sheet manufacturer literature.

q: Which polycarbonate is most used in greenhouses?
n: Twin-wall and multi-wall polycarbonate is most used in greenhouses: its hollow cells insulate, diffuse light evenly and stay stiff at low weight. Source: Polycarbonate sheet manufacturer literature.

q: What should be avoided when installing polycarbonate roofing?
n: Fasteners must not be over-tightened on polycarbonate. The sheet expands a lot with heat, so screws go through oversized holes with washers snug only, or the sheet cracks and buckles. Source: Polycarbonate sheet manufacturer installation guides.

q: Which roof has two slopes on every side?
n: A mansard roof has two slopes on every side, a steep lower slope and a flatter upper slope, giving usable attic space. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture (roof forms).

q: Which roof design typically forms a 45-degree angle?
n: Hip roofs are commonly framed so the hip rafters run at 45° in plan to the walls, with equal slopes on all sides. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (roof framing).

q: Which roof has two sloping sides meeting at a ridge?
n: A gable roof has two slopes meeting at a central ridge, with triangular gable walls at the ends. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which roof has a single slope, often used for extensions and minimalist houses?
n: A shed (lean-to or skillion) roof has a single slope. It is used for additions and minimalist houses. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture.

q: Which roof has four sloping sides and resists strong winds well?
n: A hip roof slopes on all four sides, with no tall flat gable wall to catch the wind, so it resists typhoon winds better. Source: Philippine housing guidelines on typhoon-resistant roofs; FEMA P-499 (roof shape and wind).

q: What is an advantage of cement and clay roof tiles?
n: Cement and clay roof tiles are non-combustible, so they give excellent fire resistance (Class A roof covering). Source: ASTM E108 / UL 790 (fire tests of roof coverings); roof tile manufacturer literature.

q: What type of roofing is made of thermoplastic material that bonds under heat?
n: Asphalt shingles contain thermoplastic asphalt that softens in heat: their self-seal strips bond the tabs together under the sun. Source: ARMA Residential Asphalt Roofing Manual.

q: Which roofing is typical of Mediterranean or Spanish-style architecture?
n: Barrel (S-shaped) clay tiles are the hallmark of Mediterranean and Spanish Mission style roofs. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; roof tile manufacturer literature.

q: What is a major disadvantage of ceramic roof tiles?
n: Ceramic and clay tiles weigh about 40–60 kg/m², several times a metal roof, so the roof framing must be stronger and costlier. Source: NSCP 2015 Table 204-2 (roofing dead loads); roof tile manufacturer data.
